name: Merek Thorne
source_profile:
Colonel Merek Thorne: "The Hollow Man" (LN/NE) 
Thorne himself speaks with the careful, measured authority of 
an experienced officer, seemingly unaware of the strange 
behavior of his men.  
Reputation: Many frontiersmen consider the Hollow Regiment 
a ghost story. Others believe Thorne survived the winter by 
making some terrible bargain in the mountains. 
Hidden truth: The regiment encountered the mind flayers beneath the mountains. Thorne and 
his surviving soldiers have been subjected to extensive psionic conditioning and now serve as 
unwitting agents of the illithid colony. While formerly a disciplined professional soldier, following 
his capture and psionic conditioning by the illithids, Merek’s actions no longer necessarily reflect 
his own moral judgment. There is a hope his psionic enslavement has not fundamentally 
changed his moral character. If his conditioning were broken, perhaps his original personality 
might reemerge. 
Adventure hook: A wounded soldier wearing the uniform of a northern regiment staggers into a 
frontier town. He claims to have escaped from the Hollow Regiment, but remembers nothing of 
the last two years. He begs the party to help him find his family before his colonel comes looking 
for him. 
Rivalries and uneasy alliances 
The bands comprising the Lost Banners don’t necessarily cooperate just because they all fought 
on the same side. Each band represents a different response to the defeat of the northern 
rebellion. For instance, Edric Vale despises Crowthorne for the atrocities she committed during 
the war, while Crowthorne considers Vale a coward for refusing to continue the rebellion in 
earnest. 
Sabine Rourke might occasionally hire Bennet Pike's engineers to sabotage bridges or 
fortifications, but she would never allow them near her own camp without an armed escort. 
Captain Strake might transport supplies for the Last Colours in exchange for a fee, while 
simultaneously selling information about their movements to the marquises. 
The northern marquises face an especially interesting situation. Aldric Voss and Elowen 
Harrowmont are both northern nobles who benefited from the rebellion's defeat. To the more 
ideological outlaw bands, they are living symbols of betrayal. Meanwhile, Garrus Ashford and 
Cedric Bellamy, being of southern lineage, might be more straightforward enemies in the eyes of 
former rebel soldiers.
